SECTION 01

Foundations & Human Origins

The beginnings of science and technology

01

The Emergence of Technology

PDF p. 2
  • Technology makes difficult and complicated tasks easier.
  • Technological developments are not products of a one-time thought process.
  • They come from gradual improvements to earlier works across different time periods.

Key Historical Transitions

PDF p. 3
  • Paleolithic Period
  • Neolithic Period
  • Rise of Ancient Civilizations
  • Industrial Revolution
  • The Anthropocene

The Human Revolution

PDF p. 4
  • Refers to the remarkable and sudden emergence of language, consciousness, and culture in Homo sapiens sapiens.
  • Historians call the early period of human history the Stone Age.
  • The first humans emerged from Africa and lived simultaneously with other hominid species.
  • Large, complex brains provided the capacity to make and use tools.
  • The slide dates human origins to 6 to 2 MYA.
SECTION 02

Paleolithic Age

2.5 million years ago – around 8000 BC

02

The Old Stone Age

PDF p. 5
  • The Paleolithic Age is also called the Old Stone Age.
  • It began about 2.5 million years ago and lasted until around 8000 BC.

Nomadic Way of Life

PDF p. 6–8
  • Paleolithic people were nomadic.
  • They traveled in groups or bands of about 20 or 30 members.
  • They survived through hunting and gathering.
  • They hunted buffalo, bison, wild goats, reindeer, and other animals, depending on the location.
  • They gathered wild nuts, berries, fruits, wild grains, and green plants.
  • They also fished along rivers and coastal areas.

Paleolithic Diet

PDF p. 9
  • Research cited in the module indicates that two-thirds of energy came from animal sources.
  • The Paleo Diet (caveman diet) is described as high in protein and low in carbohydrates.

Tasks, Equity & the First Families

PDF p. 10–13
  • The module assigns hunting to men and gathering to women.
  • Women generally stayed close to camp, often near water; they cared for children and searched nearby woods and meadows for berries, nuts, and grains.
  • Everyone worked to find food.
  • Some scientists believe that equity existed between Paleolithic men and women.
  • The module connects cooperation between men and women in obtaining food for themselves and their children with the emergence of the first families.

Early Tools & Flint

PDF p. 14–15
  • Paleolithic people first used technological tools and methods to perform tasks.
  • Sticks, stones, and tree branches served as early tools.
  • Flint is described as a hard, sedimentary crystalline form of the mineral quartz.
  • Hitting flint with another hard stone made it flake into sharp-edged pieces that could be used for cutting.
  • Flint technology was a major breakthrough for early people.
  • Illustrations: a hammerstone from Majuangou, China and a handaxe from Europe.

Improving Tools

PDF p. 16–18
  • Spears, bows, and arrows made hunting large animals easier.
  • Spears and fishhooks increased the number of fish caught.
  • Sharp-edged tools were used to cut plants and dig roots.
  • Scraping tools cleaned animal hides for clothing and shelter.
  • Toward the end of the Paleolithic Age, tools became smaller and sharper.
  • Animal-bone needles helped make nets and baskets and sew animal hides together for clothing.

Shelters

PDF p. 19
  • Paleolithic people learned to make shelters.
  • Tents and huts were constructed from animal skins, brush, and wood.
  • In very cold climates, some built shelters from ice and snow.
  • Many also lived in caves.

The Use of Fire

PDF p. 20–22
  • The module places the first human use of fire in the Paleolithic Age.
  • Fire supplied warmth and was used to cook food.
  • Meat smoked by fire could be stored.
  • Iron pyrite gave off sparks when struck against another rock.

Language & Knowledge

PDF p. 23
  • Spoken language developed during this age.
  • The spoken language of early people continued to grow and change.
  • Spoken communication allowed the transfer of knowledge.

Cave Paintings

PDF p. 24
  • Cave paintings have been found around the world; the slide features Lascaux, France.
  • Painters crushed yellow, black, and red rocks and combined them with animal fat.
  • They applied paints to rock walls using twigs and fingertips.
SECTION 03

Neolithic Period

10,200 BC – ending between 4500 and 2000 BC

03

First Agricultural Revolution

PDF p. 25
  • The First Agricultural Revolution was the widespread change from hunting and gathering to agriculture and settlement.
  • The Neolithic was a period in the development of human technology.
  • The module dates this period from 10,200 BC to an end between 4500 and 2000 BC.

Neolithic Society

PDF p. 27, 29
  • People lived in small tribes composed of families.
  • Tribal groups were headed by a charismatic leader.
  • The domestication of large animals resulted in a dramatic increase in social inequality.
  • The module describes Neolithic clothing as made from animal skins.
  • People relied on food produced from cultivated lands.
  • Cultivation encouraged growing settlements and surplus crop yields.

Permanent Houses

PDF p. 28
  • The growth of agriculture made permanent houses possible.
  • Mud-brick houses and stilt-house settlements were common.

Growth of Agriculture

PDF p. 30
  • Food surpluses could be stored and traded.
  • Agricultural life afforded securities.
  • Sedentary farming populations grew faster than nomadic populations.

Neolithic Technology

PDF p. 31–34
  • Examples of artifacts: bracelets, axe heads, chisels, polishing tools, projectile points, beads, and statues.
  • Neolithic stone artifacts are described as polished.
  • The slides picture a Neolithic grinding stone, sickle, and pottery.
  • The polished stone axe made large-scale forest clearance possible.
SECTION 04

Rise of Ancient Civilizations

Uses of science and technology across societies

04

Fields of Development

PDF p. 35
  • Transportation and navigation
  • Communication
  • Weapons and armors
  • Conservation of life
  • Engineering
  • Architecture

Sumerian Civilization

PDF p. 36
  • 4500 BC to 1900 BC
  • Cuneiform – handwriting
  • Uruk City
  • Irrigation and dikes
  • Sailboats
  • Wheel
  • The plow

Egyptian Civilization

PDF p. 37
  • 3100 BC to 332 BC
  • Paper or papyrus
  • Ink
  • Hieroglyphics
  • Cosmetics and wigs
  • Water clock / Clepsydra

Chinese Civilization

PDF p. 38
  • 1600 BC to 221 BC
  • Silk
  • Tea production
  • Great Wall of China
  • Gunpowder

Greek Civilization

PDF p. 39
  • 800 BC to 140 BC
  • Alarm clock
  • Water mill

Roman Civilization

PDF p. 39
  • 753 BC to 476 AD
  • Newspaper
  • Bound books / Codex
  • Roman architecture
  • Roman numerals
SECTION 05

Middle Ages & Renaissance

476 AD through the 17th century

05

The Middle “Dark” Ages

PDF p. 40
  • The Middle Ages refers to Western Europe during the postclassical era.
  • The period began with the fall of the Roman Empire in 476 AD and ended in the 1400s.
  • The Middle Ages are also called the Dark Ages.
  • The term “the West” meant Western Europe but later included America.

Problems of the Dark Ages

PDF p. 41
  • Lack of central government
  • Widespread diseases (plagues)
  • Long religious wars
  • Little to no access to education
  • Slow technological or cultural development

Technologies Listed for the Middle Ages

PDF p. 42
  • Printing press
  • Microscope
  • Telescope
  • War weapons

The Renaissance

PDF p. 43
  • The Renaissance occurred from the 14th to the 17th century.
  • It is regarded as a bridge between the Middle Ages and modern history.
  • It began as a cultural movement in Italy and spread through the rest of Europe.
SECTION 06

Industrial Revolution

Modern history • 1700s to 1900s

06

Change in Industry

PDF p. 44
  • The module places modern history and the Industrial Revolution in the 1700s to 1900s; the slide also describes an Industrial Revolution period of 1870–1900s.
  • Industry changed dramatically.
  • New inventions made life easier and had lasting effects on economies and people’s lives.

Textile Industry & Cotton Gin

PDF p. 45–46
  • Advances in the textile industry were key developments of the Industrial Revolution.
  • Eli Whitney invented the cotton gin, which increased productivity in removing seeds from cotton.
  • Spinning and weaving also experienced major gains in productivity.
  • The textile industry was among the first to employ the factory system using machines and an assembly-line approach.

Steam Engine

PDF p. 47
  • James Watt created the first truly reliable steam engine in 1775, according to the module.
  • This invention made locomotives and many textile machines possible.

Coal Mining & Iron Production

PDF p. 48–49
  • Coal mining is the process of extracting coal from the ground.
  • Coal was valued for its energy content, and industrialization greatly increased demand.
  • Replacing charcoal with coal reduced fuel costs for iron production.
  • The module states that a charcoal-powered steam engine enabled a large increase in iron production.

Machine Tools

PDF p. 50
  • The first machine tools included the screw-cutting lathe, cylinder-boring machine, and milling machine.

Use of Chemistry

PDF p. 51–52
  • Large-scale chemical production was an important Industrial Revolution development.
  • Englishman John Roebuck pioneered sulphuric acid production in 1746.
  • Chemicals were produced for fertilizers, detergents, dyes, explosives, and drugs, among other uses.
  • Germany assumed world leadership in the chemical industry, and aspiring chemists flocked to German universities.

Portland Cement

PDF p. 53
  • In 1824, British bricklayer-turned-builder Joseph Aspdin patented a chemical process for Portland cement.
  • The described process heats a clay-and-limestone mixture to approximately 1,400 °C (2,552 °F).
  • The heated material is ground to fine powder and mixed with water, sand, and gravel to produce concrete.

Agricultural Machines

PDF p. 54
  • Joseph Foljambe’s Rotherham plough (1730) was the first commercially successful iron plough.
  • Andrew Meikle invented the threshing machine in 1784.
  • The threshing machine replaced hand threshing with a flail, which had required about one-quarter of agricultural labor.

Tin Can & Canning Factory

PDF p. 55–56
  • British merchant Peter Durand patented the tin can in 1810.
  • It had an enormous effect on food preservation and transportation.
  • John Hall and Bryan Dorkin opened the first commercial canning factory in England in 1813.

Internal Combustion Engine

PDF p. 57–58
  • Jean Lenoir invented the internal combustion engine in 1858.
  • The module describes it as a heat engine in which fuel burns with an oxidizer, usually air, in a combustion chamber integral to the working-fluid flow circuit.
  • The engine was eventually used in mass transportation.

Electricity as Power

PDF p. 59
  • Scientists who contributed to the development of electricity as a power source include Benjamin Franklin, Alessandro Volta, and Michael Faraday.

Automobile

PDF p. 60
  • The module identifies Henry Ford as an important inventor in the Industrial Revolution.
  • Automobiles allowed people to travel where and when they wanted.
  • The automobile modernized the transportation industry.

Camera

PDF p. 61
  • The module credits Joseph Nicéphore Niépce, beginning in 1814, as the first person to take a photograph.

Telephone

PDF p. 62
  • Alexander Graham Bell created the telephone in 1876.
  • It improved communications and helped lead to other communications devices.

Phonograph

PDF p. 63
  • Thomas Edison created the phonograph in 1877.
  • Before the phonograph, entertainment required live musicians or actors to perform.
  • The phonograph allowed people to listen to music anywhere.

Airplane

PDF p. 64
  • Brothers Orville and Wilbur Wright created the first airplane in 1903, according to the module.
  • Within decades, airplanes transformed personal travel, business travel, and warfare.
SECTION 07

The Anthropocene

Present • The Rise of the Human Empire

07

Meaning & Origin of the Term

PDF p. 65–66
  • The Anthropocene is described as the era in which human activity is the dominant influence on climate and the environment.
  • Scientists in the Soviet Union appear to have used the term as early as the 1960s to refer to the Quaternary, the most recent geological period.
  • Atmospheric chemist Paul J. Crutzen widely popularized the term in 2000.
  • Crutzen viewed recent human influence on the atmosphere as significant enough to constitute a new geological time.

Nuclear Weapons

PDF p. 67–68
  • The module identifies nuclear weapons as one of the signs of the Anthropocene.
  • Warfare has left a mark on geology.
  • The first nuclear weapon was detonated on 16 July 1945 in New Mexico.

Fossil Fuels & Carbon Emissions

PDF p. 69–72
  • Burning fossil fuels is presented as a marker of the Anthropocene.
  • The module states that present carbon-emission rates are thought to be higher than at any point in the past 65 million years.
  • Its charts show global energy-related carbon dioxide emissions by region, greenhouse gas emissions by gas, and global carbon emissions from fossil fuels (1900–2014).

Plastic Use

PDF p. 73–74
  • Plastics were initially developed in the 1900s and their production expanded rapidly since the 1950s.
  • The module states that approximately 500 million tons of plastic are produced each year.
  • Sediments containing plastics are presented as a clear sign of the Anthropocene.
  • The slide on page 74 compares estimated decomposition times for several common discarded items.

Changed Geology

PDF p. 75–77
  • Destroying rainforest changes the future geology of Earth.
  • More than 50% of Earth’s land area has been transformed for human purposes.
  • Deforestation, farming, drilling, mining, landfills, dam-building, and coastal reclamation affect sedimentary processes.
  • These activities disrupt how layers of rock are laid down; the changes can be detected thousands of years later.
  • The visual examples include forest-cover loss in the Philippines and a landscape affected by human activity.

Use of Fertilizers

PDF p. 78
  • Efforts to feed a growing population can leave clear indicators in soil.
  • Nitrogen and phosphorus levels in soils have doubled in the last century because of increased fertilizer use.
  • The module reports production of 23.5 million tons of phosphorus each year.
  • Human activity is described as having the largest impact on the nitrogen cycle in 2.5 billion years.

Global Warming

PDF p. 79–80
  • Global warming is described as the unusually rapid increase in Earth’s average surface temperature over the past century, primarily from greenhouse gases released by burning fossil fuels.
  • The rate of temperature increase has nearly doubled in the last 50 years.
  • Average global sea levels are said to be higher than at any time in the past 115,000 years and are rising rapidly.

6th Mass Extinction

PDF p. 81
  • The moment of extinction is generally considered the death of the last individual of a species.
  • Mass extinctions caused by massive global changes are discussed as a marker of the Anthropocene.

The Dark Side of Technology

PDF p. 82–83
  • The module describes technology as mostly positive while acknowledging unsettling possibilities.
  • Michio Kaku calls such possibilities “wildcards.”
  • Unanticipated uses of science and technology could turn desirable futuristic visions into nightmares.

Closing Thought — Michio Kaku

PDF p. 84
  • “There are dangers, but only dangers if people don’t understand where technology is taking us.” — Michio Kaku
